title: Uno Platform 6.6 Adds Native AOT, Vulkan Rendering, and Broader Accessibility Support
gist: Uno Platform 6.6 pivots from design/AI tooling to runtime performance: Native AOT publishing across Android, iOS, Linux, macOS and Windows (21%-61% startup gains on .NET 10), an opt-in Vulkan Skia backend cutting per-frame render cost by up to 50%, and self-registering App/Docs MCP servers for coding agents including Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI. Accessibility for Skia-rendered apps now reaches screen readers on Windows, macOS and WebAssembly, with Android, iOS and Linux still incomplete.

insights.claim: Uno Platform 6.6 adds Native AOT publishing across five targets - Android, iOS, Linux, macOS and Windows - compiling application code ahead of time instead of relying on JIT compilation at startup.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Cross-platform .NET is closing the cold-start gap with native toolchains, weakening a long-standing argument for writing separate Swift/Kotlin apps.
insights.quote: The most significant runtime change is Native AOT support for Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows.
insights.locator: The most significant runtime change is

insights.claim: Uno measured startup improvements from Native AOT ranging from 21% on iOS to 61% on Android using its Chefs sample application on .NET 10.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: The Android-versus-iOS spread suggests Android's JIT/startup overhead was the bigger tax; Android-first consumer apps get the larger conversion-rate payoff from AOT.
insights.quote: Uno reported startup improvements ranging from 21% on iOS to 61% on Android in tests using its Chefs sample application on .NET 10

insights.claim: The reported Native AOT startup gains are vendor-run benchmarks whose results depend on application structure, hardware and deployment configuration, and JIT-based publishing remains supported alongside AOT.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Keeping JIT as a fallback signals AOT is not yet safe for all apps - expect trimming/reflection breakage to gate adoption in large codebases.
insights.quote: although results will depend on application structure, hardware, and deployment configuration. JIT-based publishing remains supported.
insights.locator: although results will depend on application structure

insights.claim: Uno Platform 6.6 introduces an opt-in Vulkan rendering backend on Windows, Linux and Android while OpenGL stays the default Skia backend on those platforms, Apple targets continue on Metal, and WebAssembly uses WebGL.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: A four-backend graphics matrix means per-platform performance testing is now mandatory; abstraction layers like Skia are where the real cross-platform moat sits.
insights.quote: OpenGL remains the default Skia backend on those platforms, while Apple targets continue using Metal and WebAssembly uses WebGL.
insights.locator: Uno Platform 6.6 also introduces an opt-in Vulkan backend

insights.claim: The Uno team reported Vulkan reduced per-frame rendering costs by as much as 50% in some tests, making it most relevant for animation-heavy or graphics-intensive applications.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: A 50% per-frame saving is the difference between 30fps and 60fps on mid-tier Android hardware - it widens the class of apps that can be built cross-platform rather than native.
insights.quote: Vulkan reduced per-frame rendering costs by as much as 50% in some tests
insights.locator: According to the Uno team, Vulkan reduced

insights.claim: Shipping Vulkan as opt-in rather than default indicates the vendor is not yet confident in driver-level stability across the Windows, Linux and Android device fleet despite the measured performance gain.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Watch whether Vulkan becomes default in 6.7/7.0 - that flip is the real signal the backend is production-grade.
insights.locator: Uno Platform 6.6 also introduces an opt-in Vulkan backend

insights.claim: Uno Platform 6.6 makes the standard WinUI presentation namespace and the x: namespace implicitly available in XAML and allows shared namespaces to be declared centrally in a GlobalNamespaces.xaml file.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Markup ergonomics are being borrowed from C#'s implicit/global usings - a sign XAML tooling is being modernised rather than deprecated.

insights.claim: Pages declaring x:Class in Uno 6.6 can now receive generated code-behind automatically, letting XAML-only pages exist without an empty .xaml.cs file, while manual code-behind stays available for constructors, event handlers and lifecycle overrides.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Fewer generated stub files means cleaner diffs and less noise for AI coding agents reading the repo - a small but compounding agent-readability win.

themes.theme: MCP servers auto-registering with coding agents

insights.claim: Uno's App MCP and Docs MCP servers can now register themselves automatically with supported development agents including Visual Studio and VS Code Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, though not all agents support it yet.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Framework vendors are now shipping directly into the agent tool-surface; MCP registration is becoming a distribution channel, and the named agent list is a de facto market-share ranking.
insights.quote: Automatic registration is supported for tools including Visual Studio and VS Code Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI, but not all agents support it yet.
insights.locator: For AI-assisted workflows, Uno's App MCP

insights.claim: The App MCP server exposes a running application to an AI agent for live inspection and interaction, while the Docs MCP server supplies current framework documentation to the agent.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: The runtime-inspection MCP is the harder-to-copy asset: it moves agents from writing code to observing the app they wrote, closing the feedback loop that limits agentic UI work.
insights.quote: The App MCP exposes a running application to an agent for inspection and interaction, while the Docs MCP provides access to current Uno documentation.
insights.locator: The App MCP exposes a running application

insights.claim: Screen readers can now access Uno interfaces rendered through Skia on Windows, macOS and WebAssembly, but Android and iOS support remains in progress and Linux support is only planned.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Custom-rendered UI frameworks carry an accessibility debt that blocks public-sector and regulated-enterprise procurement - the missing mobile support is a live sales objection.
insights.quote: Screen readers can now access Uno interfaces on Windows, macOS, and WebAssembly. Android and iOS support remains in progress, while Linux support is planned.

insights.claim: Uno 6.6 delivers complete Input Method Editor composition for multi-keystroke Asian languages across all principal targets plus automatic font fallback for interfaces mixing multiple writing systems.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Full IME support is the gating requirement for shipping into Japanese, Chinese and Korean markets - this unlocks Asia-Pacific enterprise deployments previously off the table.
insights.locator: The release additionally provides complete Input Method Editor composition

insights.claim: Uno Platform 6.6 broadens WinUI compatibility with APIs for projections, geometry transforms, text highlighting, spell checking, flyouts, clipboard operations, drag and drop and WebView2, plus animated WebP playback and Mica and Acrylic backdrops on macOS.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: The remaining work is long-tail API parity rather than architecture - the framework is in a catch-up grind against a moving Microsoft target.

insights.claim: Support levels for the newly added WinUI APIs vary by target platform, so applications depending on them must review platform-specific notes rather than assume uniform behaviour.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Write-once-run-anywhere remains conditional; the hidden cost of cross-platform frameworks stays in per-target QA, not in the initial build.
insights.quote: The exact support level varies by target, so applications relying on these APIs should review the platform-specific notes.
insights.locator: The exact support level varies by target

insights.claim: Uno 6.6 keeps SkiaSharp 3.x as the default while offering SkiaSharp 4.x as an opt-in dependency, and upgrading applications must update the Uno SDK entry in global.json and follow the migration guide.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: Deferring the SkiaSharp 4 default means a second breaking-change wave is still queued - budget migration effort for the next release, not this one.
insights.quote: SkiaSharp 4.x is available as an opt-in dependency, while Uno 6.6 continues to use SkiaSharp 3.x by default.
insights.locator: SkiaSharp 4.x is available as an opt-in dependency

insights.claim: Uno's recent release cadence shifted from visual design and AI-assisted development tooling in prior versions toward runtime performance and closing WinUI API gaps on Skia-based targets in 6.6.
insights.speaker: Edin Kapić
insights.so_what: A vendor rotating from feature marketing back to runtime fundamentals usually signals enterprise buyers pushed back on performance - a leading indicator of real production adoption.
insights.quote: Version 6.6 focuses more heavily on runtime performance and filling gaps between WinUI APIs and Uno’s Skia-based targets.
insights.locator: Recent releases have also added visual design
